design.title: CAVR-Dyna — Change-Aware Stochastic Model-Based RL for Dynamic Mazes

slides.title: Section 01 — Problem & Method
slides.task_brief: Section divider. Giant faint chapter numeral '01' (font-num, ~200px, color rgba(255,255,255,0.06)) positioned right side. Kicker: 'SECTION 01 / 03'. Title (h1): 'Problem & Method'. Tagline (muted, one sentence): 'Why classical Dyna breaks the moment the maze changes — and the five mechanisms CAVR-Dyna adds to survive it.' Small progress dots or hairline list of the three sections at bottom: 01 Problem & Method (highlighted, accent), 02 Empirical Evidence, 03 Deliverables & Limits.

slides.title: The problem: navigation that changes under you
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'PROBLEM STATEMENT'. Title: 'Navigation that changes while you are learning it'. Left column body (two paragraphs, verbatim): (1) 'The agent acts in a 9×9 grid maze formalized as an MDP M = ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩. Actions slip: with probability 1−ρ the intended move executes, otherwise a uniformly random passable move — so even the transition table is stochastic before the world starts changing.' (2) 'Topology then changes mid-run: edges get blocked or hidden shortcuts open at evaluator-chosen times, invisible to the agent (leak guard: only (s, a, r, s′) tuples are exposed). A Dyna agent that trusts its learned model keeps re-using stale experience precisely where the world moved — adaptation delay explodes.' Three stat cards across the bottom (num font, big value + label): 'ρ ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.3}' / 'action slip levels evaluated', '{blocking, shortcut, static}' / 'change scenarios', '640' / 'pilot runs · 8 map/seed pairs'. Add a small note line (micro, faint): 'Success measured post-change; adaptation delay = steps until rolling success recovers, censoring-aware.'

slides.title: Method: five mechanisms
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'METHOD'. Title: 'Five mechanisms, one repair loop'. Bento grid of five cards (2 rows: 3 + 2), each with a num-font index, bold name, and 2-line description (verbatim): (1) 'Categorical Dirichlet model — per-(s,a) outcome counts give expected transitions and rewards under slip; a factored edge-belief map tracks per-edge log-odds of being open.' (2) 'Calibrated CUSUM detector — two-level change detection on the FROZEN pre-update prediction; per-(s,a) alarms with false-alarm budget enforced by design.' (3) 'Repair: local forgetting — on alarm, forget the affected model region (epoch bump) so stale experience stops poisoning planning.' (4) 'Counterfactual prioritized backups — goal-conditioned expected value of each repair pushes backups through an epoch-versioned priority heap; stale entries invalidate automatically.' (5) 'VoC budget + exploration floor — value-of-computation-style arbiter picks the backup budget B ∈ {0, 8, 16, 32, 64}; a nonzero ε-floor keeps hidden shortcuts rediscoverable.' Accent-highlight card 2 (detector) and card 5 (budget) borders subtly with --accent.

slides.title: Design: modules & frozen hyperparameters
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'SOFTWARE DESIGN'. Title: 'Module inventory and frozen configuration'. Left card: table.deck 'Module / Responsibility' rows (verbatim): 'envs/ — grid env, maze gen, change scenarios'; 'models/ — Dirichlet model, edge beliefs, episodic map, CUSUM detector'; 'agents/ — q_learning, dyna_q(+), prioritized sweeping, stochastic dyna, dstar_lite, cavr (+ 2 ablations)'; 'planning/ — versioned heap, counterfactual, probes, budget'; 'evaluation/ — runner, metrics, statistics, oracles, calibration'; 'tests/ — 41 unit tests'. Right card: table.deck 'Hyperparameter / Value' rows (from checkpoint agent_cfg, verbatim): 'α (learning rate) — 0.1', 'α_model — 0.15', 'γ (discount) — 0.97', 'ε (exploration floor) — 0.1', 'Dyna n — 20', 'local-forgetting n — 32', 'budget cap — 64', 'CUSUM h — 4.0', 'drift κ — 0.0003', 'probe θ_probe — 0.12'. Footer note (micro): 'Seeds fixed per manifest; procedural mazes are content-hashed (SHA256) so any run can be reproduced bit-for-bit.'

slides.title: Protocol & calibration
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'EXPERIMENTAL PROTOCOL'. Title: 'Calibrate first, then compare ten methods'. Left column card, body verbatim: 'Before any comparison, the detector is calibrated on validation mazes (seeds 1004–1007, disjoint from training seeds 1000–1003): the CUSUM threshold h sets the false-alarm budget, and the repair gain κ sets how aggressively counters are re-armed after an alarm. Both are chosen from measured grids, not heuristics.' Below: two compact table.deck tables. Table A 'CUSUM threshold grid' rows verbatim: h=3.0 → FA/1000 5.63; h=4.0 → 2.50 (highlight row, accent, label 'chosen'); h=5.0 → 0.83; h=6.0 → 0.42; h=8.0 → 0.00; h=10.0 → 0.00. Table B 'Repair gain κ grid': κ=0.0003 → mean delay 498 (highlight 'chosen'); κ=0.001 → 510.5; κ=0.003 → 750. Right column: a 'chosen configuration' card with badge-pass 'h = 4.0 — ≤ 2.5 false alarms / 1000 steps' and 'κ = 0.0003 — fastest mean repair delay', plus a short paragraph (verbatim): 'The full grid then compares 10 methods across 8 conditions — {blocking, shortcut, static} × ρ ∈ {0, 0.1, 0.3} — over 8 map/seed pairs: CAVR, two CAVR ablations (no-detector, fixed budget B=32), D* Lite, Dirichlet Dyna, local-forgetting Dyna, Dyna-Q, Dyna-Q+, prioritized sweeping and Q-learning, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals across pairs.'

slides.title: Headline result: faster adaptation
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'HEADLINE RESULT'. Title: 'CAVR cuts post-change adaptation delay by 47–52%'. Left: three stacked stat cards (verbatim numbers): '−47–52%' / 'median adaptation delay vs strongest Dyna baseline (local_forgetting) at ρ=0.3 — paired bootstrap CI excludes zero'; '≤ 2.7 / 1000' / 'false alarms at ρ=0.3, inside the G1 budget of 5/1000'; 'G2: PARTIAL' (amber) / 'a credible steady-state success cost remains — reported, not hidden'. Right: figframe image 'fig_adaptation_bar.png' (relative path, white card frame) with caption (micro, muted): 'Median adaptation delay with 95% bootstrap CI — blocking (left) and shortcut (right) scenarios; CAVR highlighted.'

slides.title: Learning curves & per-condition table
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'PILOT GRID'. Title: 'Rolling success through a blocking event'. Left (wide): figframe image 'fig_learning_curves.png' (relative path) caption: 'Blocking, ρ=0.3: rolling success (window 8 episodes); dotted marker = topology change. All ten methods, same seeds.' Right: compact table.deck titled 'Blocking · ρ=0.3' with rows verbatim (method / success / succ_post / delay_med / plan_ms): cavr 0.445 0.616 82 4412 (highlight); dstar_lite 0.726 0.674 54 161; dirichlet_dyna 0.512 0.606 155 0; local_forgetting 0.479 0.590 152 0; dyna_q 0.404 0.491 113 0; q_learning 0.358 0.453 142 0. Footer note (micro): 'D* Lite leads this condition — published as measured; CAVR trades planning wall-clock for model-based adaptation that needs no replanning oracle.'

slides.title: Compute vs adaptation
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'TRADE-OFF'. Title: 'Compute buys adaptation — the Pareto view'. Left: figframe image 'fig_pareto.png' (relative path) caption: 'Blocking, ρ=0.3: median post-change adaptation delay vs mean planning wall-clock per run (log scale).' Right: four num-font stat rows (verbatim): 'cavr — 82 steps @ 4412 ms', 'dstar_lite — 54 steps @ 161 ms', 'cavr_nodetector — 130 steps @ 2372 ms', 'cavr_fixedB — 399 steps @ 3793 ms'. Below, one short paragraph (verbatim): 'Removing the detector doubles the delay; fixing the budget B=32 nearly quintuples it while spending the same compute — the adaptive arbiter, not raw planning depth, is what buys fast recovery.'

slides.title: Detector behaviour
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'CHANGE DETECTION'. Title: 'Alarms stay rare — and fire when it matters'. Left: figframe image 'fig_detector.png' (relative path) caption: 'Left: false alarms per 1000 stationary steps vs slip ρ (dashed = G1 budget 5/1000). Right: mean detection delay on changed runs.' Right column body verbatim: 'On stationary runs the calibrated CUSUM stays within budget at every slip level — 0.8 FA/1000 at ρ=0.1 rising to 1.5 at ρ=0.3, against the 5/1000 ceiling. On changed runs it localizes the break: mean detection delay ≈ 70 steps at ρ=0.3. Alarms are computed on the frozen pre-update prediction, so the detector cannot hide its own learning signal.' Add two chip pills: '0.8 FA/1000 @ ρ=0.1' and '≈70 steps detection @ ρ=0.3'.

slides.title: Held-out verification: V1–V4 PASS
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'VERIFICATION'. Title: 'Trained weights verified on unseen schedules'. Top row: four badge-pass pills verbatim: 'V1 stationarity + success — PASS', 'V2 adaptation — PASS', 'V3 model sanity — PASS', 'V4 determinism — PASS'. Table.deck 'Held-out runs (verify slip ρ=0.3, unseen edge/time schedules)' columns maze / static success / adaptation delay / alarms / max|Σp−1| rows verbatim: 1000 — 1.00 — 503 — 6 — 2.22e-16; 1001 — 1.00 — 11 — 9 — 2.22e-16; 1002 — 0.97 — 6 — 7 — 2.22e-16; 1003 — 1.00 — 44 — 7 — 2.22e-16. Footer paragraph verbatim: 'Verification re-runs the saved checkpoints under NEW schedules chosen by the evaluator at a harsher slip (0.3 vs 0.1 in training). All four gates pass; model probabilities sum to machine precision and reloaded weights replay bit-identically.'

slides.title: Honest limits & known defects
slides.layout: split: limits list + belief heatmap figure
slides.task_brief: Kicker: 'LIMITATIONS'. Title: 'What the evidence does not support (yet)'. Left: three numbered limit cards (verbatim): (1) 'Steady-state cost — CAVR pays a credible success-rate cost once the world is static again (G2 verdict PARTIAL): e.g. blocking ρ=0.3 success 0.445 vs D* Lite 0.726.' (2) 'D* Lite wins several regimes — with a true map oracle it is faster and near-perfect; CAVR is the right tool only when walls must be learned, not given.' (3) 'Belief-map blind spots — under MAP beliefs two of 81 cells stay unreachable from the start after the blocking event; the detector repairs visited corridors, not every pocket.' Right: figframe image 'fig_belief_heatmap.png' (relative path) caption verbatim: 'Learned edge-open beliefs for maze 1000. The left evaluator-view panel renders blank in the shipped artifact — a known plotting defect we ship as-is rather than disguise.'
